extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; readers of historical accounts of the colonial press
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria and practical standards described in a history of early American printing and journalism (Bradfords, Franklin, Zenger), covering content choices, legal constraints, editorial practice, libel law, and the press's civic role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content focus of early newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: Like the New England papers, it printed little of the local news, with which everybody was supposed to be conversant, but was made up principally of extracts from foreign journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early weeklies tended to favor reprints/extracts from foreign journals over original local reporting; typical format/size and weekly schedule shaped content choices and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors surveil and defend each other
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors, even in those early days when there were but three or four of them and they were far apart, were watching each other; and ... Andrew Bradford ... was defending the New England Courant and its publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial networks mattered: newspapers monitored peers and publicly defended one another, shaping inter-paper alliances and norms of mutual support in disputes with authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorials as defense of free press
rubrics_metrics.description: The first newspaper defense of a free press: 'My Lord Coke observes ... that to punish first, and then inquire, the law abhors;' Bradford used this line to criticize punitive government action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial writing could explicitly assert legal and moral arguments for press freedom (e.g., condemning punishment prior to inquiry); such editorials functioned as principled defenses against censorship and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal requirement: obtain a printing license
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the first instructions given to Governor Dongan in 1686 was to see that no one did any printing without first obtaining a license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printers operated under explicit colonial licensing rules; legal compliance (licenses) was a precondition to operate and shaped who could publish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government printing contracts and obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Council passed a resolution offering a salary 'to any printer who would settle in the colony and print the Acts of Assembly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printers could be recruited/paid to print government acts; such arrangements created contractual obligations and sometimes political tensions when officials expected additional favors or content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish public papers from private documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Bradford refused to print [the governor's report], as he considered it a private diary and not a public paper coming within his contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printers exercised judgment about what constituted public material appropriate for publication versus private materials outside their duties; refusal could provoke official reprisals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as platform to air grievances and organize opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Those opposed to the interests of the Crown attempted to use the press ... the opposition decided to have their own paper ... they brought out the New York Weekly Journal ... filled with direct allusions to Cosby and his conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers were deliberately used to publicize grievances, ridicule maladministration, and mobilize political opposition; editors and contributors expected political impact (and risked official sanction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of libel under contemporary law (Holt)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If people should not be called to account for possessing the people with an ill opinion of the government, no government can subsist.' (Law treated publications that produced ill opinion of government as seditious.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the prevailing English/colonial law, libel/seditious offenses were judged by whether publications tended to weaken the authority of magistrates; truth could be legally constrained as a defense and courts often resisted defenses appealing to truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury power and community sentiment can override law
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamilton appealed to the feeling in the community ... the jury returned a verdict of 'Not guilty' — acquitting Zenger despite the strict law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical outcomes in libel trials could depend on jury sentiment and community standards; juries could deliver general verdicts that effectively protected press expression even when statutory law seemed adverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial continuity and resilience under repression
rubrics_metrics.description: Zenger edited his paper in jail ... promised 'by the liberty of speaking to my servants through the hole of the door of the prison to entertain you with my weekly journal as formerly,' and did so until the trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining publication under adverse conditions (imprisonment, denial of materials) was a practiced resilience; sustaining the paper signaled commitment and could galvanize public support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business viability metrics: subscribers and advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Keimer's paper struggled until circulation was reduced to ninety subscribers and was sold ... there was no visible evidence of increased advertising after Zenger's trial, and son John Zenger later complained of delinquent subscribers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical success depended on subscriber numbers and advertising revenue; political prominence did not automatically translate into commercial gain, and delinquent subscriptions threatened viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training, style, and intellectual bent of editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Franklin ... studied style by copying Addison and Steele ... he had interesting and intensive training ... and the philosophical bent that he showed ... was now to be given full sway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial skill came from deliberate study and experience; stylistic training and intellectual formation helped editors shape persuasive, influential journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and risks of anonymous contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers 47, 48 and 49 were primarily taken up with the publication of an anonymous letter ... purporting to be from a New Jersey settler who ... criticized the maladministration of Governor Cosby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymous pieces could be powerful tools for criticism but exposed publishers and printers to accusations of seditious libel and official reprisals (e.g., proclamations, arrests, burning of issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Press's civic role: promote democracy and national sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Development of journalism in connection with democracy — Growth of spirit of nationality ... the history of journalism is ... of that power and of those wielding it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism was portrayed as an institutional force closely tied to democratic development and national identity; editors and papers were judged by their contribution to public liberty and civic discourse.
